text: The CDO Data Science team aims to establish a flexible AI and data science cloud computing environment (sandbox) at the Protected B level. This environment is designed to support agile experimentation, rapid prototyping, and secure data analysis across a range of CDO-led AI and data missions. A key objective is to accelerate the Authorization to Operate (ATO) for cloud-based AI components as part of the broader Enterprise AI Strategy. This includes enabling retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflows, vector-based search, and other advanced AI capabilities within a secure, scalable, and cost-effective framework. In doing so, the initiative contributes to the broader goals of the Enterprise AI Strategy by fostering responsible AI innovation, supporting reusable solutions, and ensuring compliant handling of protected data across Health Canada and PHAC.

Need functional and freedom
Modifying policies and operational models to better suit the needs data scientists. 
Break job classification barriers as it relates to coding.

Scientists should be able to independently select and evaluate tools.
Expert Community and Budgeting
Build and rely on an expert community to assist with collaboration,  problem-solving and security. 
Implement a ceiling price strategy to prevent budget issues, and purchase credits to avoid shutdowns while seeking new funding. 
Leverage Successful Project Models
Use successful projects as templates for future endeavors, minimizing repetitive approvals.
Once  infrastructure and tools have ATO (Authority to Operate), they should be used as building blocks with minimal re-approval, and there will be some edge cases.

Data engineers don’t fit standard job categories; they are more aligned with Computer System Engineers, focusing on efficient resource use.

Shift security focus from gatekeeping and report to auditing and visibility
Leverage automated patching and containerized environments for security.
Data science relies heavily on open-source tools, which differs in security management from proprietary software.
Trusted People, Data, and Environments: Acknowledge that having all three is rare; guide teams on security risk assessment and provide exception processes.

Notes from meeting with Dan
Wants to support the CDO RAG IT initiative as best as he can.
For HPFB RMOD Data Science group to use the RAG IT environment it need same level of functionality and freedom as the high resiliency environment (HRE). 
Some concerns and issues were express about the initiative that could be addressed with modified policies and operation models. 
The whole idea that there are only certain job classifications and organizations who cade code needs to change.
Most Data Science is done with open source. The HRE is built with open source. 
The way security is managed between open source and proprietary software is quire different. 
Security needs more emphasis on visibility auditing less on writing reports and gatekeeping. Get right people to write the correct rationales.
The line between personal productivity and analysis to enterprise architecture is a spectrum, not a line. Data science analysis projects are not IP projects and expecting a data scientist to create a concept of operations and an architecture to do a one of analysis of some data does not work.
Scientists have to be able to select and evaluate their own tools, it's part of the job
Base architecture, can do a lot by following on with what they do and how they have automated patching in the HRE. Containers and container management - very amenable to auditinh and daily patching. HPFB uses service based contracts for continuous security patching for HRE - flat rate contract. All base OS, crypto, java, etc. all patched with high level confidence. 
Where is the right balance between "new software to run right now vs needing to hire a consultant to investigate"?
Have trusted people, trusted data, trusted environment. Unreasonable to expect all three. Usually ok to accept two out of three. Need clear guidance for assessing security risk, and an exception process. 
Once you have done one successful project learn from it and you can use this as a template for future projects. 
TBS policies are generally not that restrictive. Issue is the assessment processes or forms that we  need to fill out to allocate risk to either users or vendors. 
Once the pieces of infrastructure and tools have an ATO they become building blocks and in general you should be able to assemble them as needed and there will be edge cases where an ATO may be required but in general you should be able to handle them with a combination of guidelines and relying on your people to structure things in a sensile way. Need this to change to allow for other ways to solve these problems.
We should also create and rely on a community of experts in this field to help people work together. 
Ceiling price that you aren't going to hit but aren't going to get cut off.
Credits purchased to prevent getting shut down while looking for new funding.
Data Engineers do not fit in any of the GoC job classifications. They are not CS or IT. The are Computer System Engineers. Engineering side - how to use these resources efficiently
 
Automated testing? 
need to do it in a networked way - integration testing
 
 
 
Something really critical that can't build themselves - platform agnostic identity service
Without one we have to replicate it in every service and keep it in sync

Problème
Les équipes de science des données et les scientifiques de Santé Canada sont freinés par la difficulté de se procurer et d'utiliser les outils de science des données et les ressources informatiques de haute performance couramment disponibles.
Ces équipes ont souvent recours à d'autres environnements pour expérimenter, ce qui ajoute au risque et à l'inefficacité.
Le manque d'environnements « Bac à sable » dédiés étouffe l'innovation et retarde les projets, ce qui a un impact négatif sur la productivité, les coûts et la fidélisation des scientifiques des données.
En l'absence d'une architecture de solution unifiée, chaque projet de science des données est contraint de développer sa propre architecture, ce qui conduit à l'inefficacité et à un retour sur investissement plus faible. | 
Opportunité
Permettre aux équipes et aux scientifiques de la science des données de disposer d'environnements de science des données flexibles, disponibles, rapides, agiles et évolutifs. 
Amélioration de la gestion des logiciels et des outils de science des données et des processus.
Amélioration du service aux praticiens de la science des données grâce à la visibilité et à une voix commune.
Augmenter la valeur des données Protégé B grâce à l'intelligence artificielle (IA) et à l'analyse avancée. |

Suivre les projets ayant des composantes similaires pour progresser. | 
La communauté de pratique en matière d’IA n'est pas en mesure de parvenir à un consensus : Les scientifiques des données ont des opinions bien arrêtées sur les outils et les environnements, qui vont souvent à l'encontre des orientations de l'entreprise. Il se peut qu'ils ne soient pas attirés par le service dans son ensemble. | Continuer à impliquer la communauté de pratique en matière d'IA et tenir compte de son point de vue lors de la conception (centrée sur l'utilisateur).

Hi Patrick,

 

Thank you again for coming to ARB July 9, 2024.   Please find the draft Record of Decisions for your review before publishing.     Any feedback / corrections / clarifications are appreciated.  

 

===>

The Office of the Chief Data Office has identified the need to establish a Data Science Environment for data scientists and data science initiatives.

 

This environment will be able to quickly stand-up scalable data science environments, in the cloud and on-premises, which will be leveraged by multiple priority list projects starting with RAGnalysis.

 

A Data Science Environment will enhance the efficiency, innovation, and collaboration of Health Canada's data science teams by: streamlining data science software approval processes, providing dedicated sandbox environments, providing approved data science software including Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning, establishing flexible infrastructure including cloud / git repositories / on-premises servers / Graphic Processing Units / desktop software, and granting necessary administrative privileges to data scientists while respecting proper accountability .  

 

The proposed environment is based on Data Science team prototypes and engagements and is based on desktop, cloud, vendor specific cloud components, (such as MS Fabric) and On-Prem Server.   The conceptual target architecture layers for the Data Science environment (iHUB) are Access, Security & Privacy, Storage, Compute and Services. 

 

Discussion/considerations:

 

*       Clarify usage of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to address Generative AI and Decision Making AI. 

*       Include AI capabilities/technologies as a Development Software standard for review by Development Software Advisory Table.  

*       Consult with DPDDMD regarding the guardrails being identified for Citizen Development to mitigate the building of unmanaged legacy files and follow the product lifecycle management to minimize technical debt. 

*       From a security perspective, there are challenges with the current environments and unmanaged devices that are being worked on to be addressed.  For a Data Science environment, with large data volume and analysis, emphasis must be on data security and ensuring data is not inadvertently shared outside of the environment. 

*       Data Science community perspective is that there needs to be improvements in IT service for data science work, especially in the labs and enabling the science community.  Labs are working on documentation regarding their activities, resources, locations and IT software/hardware posture to assist DTB in understanding/servicing the science community.

Executive Summary


Purpose
The purpose of this document is to capture the high-level business requirements (business/stakeholder) to perform preliminary options analysis on possible technical solutions. 
The resulting document should be read and understood by all key stakeholders and project team members to build consensus on the scope of the technical solution.

Detailed Business Context
Business Need
The following business needs were identified through:
Insights from the CDO’s work on implementing Generative AI experiments;
Discussions with AI practitioners, data scientists, and scientists throughout the department;
The experiences of the Office of the Chief Data Officer, data scientists’ work with clients to leverage their data using AI, machine learning, and natural language processing.
The enterprise's data science and IT teams face significant challenges due to the lack of advanced data science tools, availability of high-performance computing resources, dedicated environments for experimentation and data analysis, and a lack of an overall solution architecture. These obstacles hinder the organization’s ability to quickly and efficiently leverage data and advanced analytics, particularly with rapidly evolving AI and ML techniques and tools. Addressing these challenges is crucial for maintaining trust, being viewed as a 21st-century partner and regulator, fostering innovation, and ensuring efficient and defensible data-driven decision-making.
By addressing the following business needs, Health Canada can overcome the current challenges faced by its data science, scientists and IT teams, fostering an environment that supports innovation, efficiency, and effective data-driven decision-making. 
A data science platform with a modular and extensible architecture that facilitates the use of open-source software, in line the TBS guidance to prioritize the use of open-source software as well as open standards.
Empower data scientists and scientists throughout the department with more available computing, access to current technologies, and enabling more sophisticated DevOps and MLOps methodologies. 
Improved retention of data scientists as AI technologies and services used by private companies and academia are increasingly available externally, not internally. 
Fully leverage existing infrastructure and services for data integration and data pipelines, including data collection from external sources and making these datasets available internally for use in the environment. 
Enable more efficient and effective data science work and experimentation. This includes easily provisioned sandbox environments for experiments and innovation, support for advanced AI/ML projects, and more support for program areas to leverage AI and their data.
Ability for the CDO data science team to collaborate internally and externally on common AI use cases and reuse existing code and solutions. 
Streamlined approval process for computing resources and software, significantly reducing delays in data analysis work. Users benefit from self-serve access to pre-approved free software and a clear and transparent process for procuring licenses for pre-approved paid software.
Data scientists and managers can efficiently request and access an up-to-date suite of data science tools through a streamlined process.
Enable the deployment of workloads across desktop, on-premises, and cloud environments, ensuring flexible and scalable computing capabilities.
Stakeholder Analysis
The RAG IT project, to enhance the data science infrastructure, will impact a wide range of stakeholders within the organization. This section outlines how each stakeholder group may be affected, their participation in the project, and their needs throughout the business analysis activities.
Current Applications and Technology
Despite having a wide array of advanced technologies at our disposal, they often are implemented as distinct and separate tools and solutions, and as a result often fail to meet the needs of the data science community for an integrated work environment. The current landscape features a range of powerful tools and systems, from Microsoft Fabric Lakehouse and Python Notebooks to version control with Git, data pipelines with Kafka, and containerization through Docker and Kubernetes. While each of these tools has been implemented to serve a specific purpose and function there is an overall lack of cohesion when performing data related tasks which negatively impacts efficient data science work. As a result, despite the availability of these technologies and services data scientists face challenges in navigating disparate systems, managing transitions between environments, and maintaining consistent workflows, limiting their ability to leverage these tools to their full potential. A concrete example this is code version control. Code version control functionality is available through multiple platforms like Git, GitHub.com, HC’s GitHub Enterprise, SSC’s GCcode, and HC’s Azure DevOps, and can be accessed via desktop command line tools, GitHub Desktop, and GitKraken. However each solution has its own pros and cons for version control on collaborative projects.

As discussed in the previous section, although some infrastructure and tools are available at Health Canada, Data Science teams, they are hindered by a combination of lengthy approval processes, out of date software, and a lack of appropriate flexible infrastructure for their work.
The current IT related processes at Health Canada significantly inhibit collaborative data science work. Data science teams and scientists face challenges in procuring and using commonly available data science tools and high-performance computing resources, which are essential for deriving insights from data, modeling, transformation, and analysis to support informed decision-making. The existing approval processes, originally designed for governing business application development and deployment, delay and obstruct efficient and timely data analysis work. 
Additionally, the department lacks dedicated, persistent "Sandbox" environments for prototyping and innovation, forcing teams to rely on external computing resources or unmanaged IT solutions, each with inherent limitations and risks. Data scientists are also restricted in managing their own environments and lack the necessary administrative privileges to tailor their tools to specific project needs and explore cutting-edge AI and ML solutions for addressing business challenges. This lack of resources, flexibility, and environment for innovation and experimentation stifles innovation, reduces overall efficiency, and impedes retention. Furthermore, without a unified solution architecture in place, each data science project is forced to develop its own unique architecture, leading to inefficiencies and inconsistencies across projects.

STATEMENT OF SENSITIVITY (SOS)

Data Science Environment Proposal
Context

Background
Today's data science and analytics initiatives demand quick, agile and scalable environments that enable the use of the latest data science software and tools. Development in this paradigm requires teams to focus on developing Minimally Viable Products (MVPs) as quickly as possible and to perform frequent iterations to refine them. This document proposes a prototyping, experimentation, and analysis environment for the Data Science Team within the Chief Data Office (CDO). This proposal may also have utility for other data science or science teams within the department. This proposal has been developed out of the lessons learned by the CDO Data Science Team from several previous and in-progress projects. Those projects are the bases of the use cases discussed in the “Current State and Business Needs” section.
Current State and Business Need(s)
The work of data science teams within Health Canada, and the department’s science teams, often involves the need for niche tools and higher performance computing. This type of work necessitates flexibility so that workers can complete their projects. The processes for requesting new software, for example, or other IT resources can involve relatively long processes for seeking approval and support for these types of work. Additionally, the department currently lacks “Sandbox” environments for performing prototyping or other innovation type work. Instead, teams tend to use computing resources outside of DTB’s offerings, such as unmanaged workstations, or temporary cloud computing though Shared Services Canada (SSC) Science Cloud. Other approaches include using managed desktops or laptops for this type of work, perhaps with Sci Ops accounts for local admin, or the department’s new Microsoft Fabric service. The data science team, in working on their projects, have found that each of the different current approaches have various advantages and disadvantages. Examples of these projects are described below.
COVID-Lessons Learned Library: In support of the broader COVID-Lessons Learned Library project, the data science team within the CDO was tasked with performing document analysis on candidate documents to help determine if they should be included in the library. Faced with very tight deadlines and a lack of any practical alternatives for performing analysis on a large volume of Protected B files (approx. 180,000 files), the team performed the analysis using custom Python scripts developed and running on their managed laptop computers. The data was accessed directly from a network share drive and the source code was maintained using Health Canada’s GitHub Enterprise service. Although the project was successful, there were several significant challenges faced by the team. These included:
Access to Data: The data was stored on shared network drives. Accessing this data required transferring files to local computers over the VPN. Due to the large number of files this was a significant bottleneck.
Lack of computing environment: Early in the project, a significant effort was made to find a computing environment that was suitable for a large number of Protected files where the data science team could implement and run their custom analysis code. Unfortunately, no corporate Health Canada environment was available, nor was any environment with either Statistics Canada or Shared Services Canada (SSC).
Long processing times: Without a computing environment, the data science team performed the analysis by running their custom scripts on their managed laptops. Due to the massive volume of data being processed, the team split the files into groups so that each member of the team could process in parallel with each other. This added an additional logistics element to the project. Despite this collaboration on the team, it still took several weeks to process the data.
Lack of privileges on GitHub Enterprise: The team made use of Health Canada’s GitHub Enterprise system to maintain and collaborate on their analysis scripts. Although this provides a valuable service, team members were not able to create their own accounts on this service. Furthermore, the team lacked the needed permissions to create their own project (other than one attached to one of the team members’ usernames). Lastly, there were no “runners” available on GitHub Enterprise for running the team’s test cases automatically.

Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) Library and Analysis: After the completion of the COVID-Lessons Learned Library project, the data science team has received several requests for similar Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) type projects. Building on the COVID-LLL work, the data science team has written a Python Library for document processing, including transcription of audio files, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) using Tesseract, reading the contents and metadata, and calculating the similarity between files of a wide variety of file types. To make full use of this library, it needs to be run with several system dependencies installed locally on the machine or run in a container with these dependencies installed. Although it improves on several of the challenges from the COVID-Lessons Learned Library project, running this library on larger data sets, as well as installing the system dependencies can still be a challenge without a dedicated environment to run the analysis. Currently all work on this initiative is completed on managed laptops.

Table Data Extraction Experiments: Somewhat related to the theme of Intelligent Document Processing, the data science team has performed experiments on automatic extraction of tabular data from scanned documents. This involved using AI models to detect tables and their structure and Tesseract OCR to extract the scanned text. This experiment was performed on managed laptops. Although the laptops used were very high performing, it still took significant time to run the experiments without a more appropriate environment for this work.

Chat-GPT for Science Literature Experiments: In response to significant interest within the department in Chat-GPT, the data science team performed a study on the effectiveness of the GPT-3.5 model for various data extraction and summarization use cases with scientific literature. This work was completed using a combination of local development and the SSC Science Cloud environment, which provided access to a subscription in Azure for the data science team to set up and run the experiments. Although the SSC Science environment was sufficient for this experiment, it was limited to working at the unclassified level and time limited to a short duration experiment before being taken offline.

RAGNalysis: Building from the Chat-GPT experiments, the RAGNalysis project, currently in flight, is testing the effectiveness of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Large Language Models (LLMs) for answering questions about internal documentation. These models promise improved responses thanks to the ability to provide highly relevant context-specific responses and cite sources from provided content when responding to prompts. This experiment includes testing models provided via APIs in addition to models that can be run “locally”. It also aims to test and demonstrate a connection to Microsoft Fabric, examining the capabilities of that environment. The RAG models and experiments are primarily being executed on an Azure tenant set up by SSC Science Could and being configured by the data science team. The experiment is being developed for maximum flexibility, utilizing container services wherever possible so that the resulting code could run on premises if needed. Many design choices have been inspired by the GPHIN team, out of interest for the CDO data science team to maintain similar technical capacity. Additional details of this project are provided in the Reference Materials section of this document.

Target State and Desired Outcomes
Data science teams and scientific teams within Health Canada require flexile computing environments for performing agile experiments, prototyping, and analysis at the Protected B level. These teams also require sufficient permissions to setup their own projects and have flexibility to use tools and approaches that are suitable for a given project. Key outcomes are listed below:
Data science and scientific teams have environments and tools needed to work on their projects.
Supported by clear best practices, maintained templates, example projects, and tailored governance policies, teams can provision their own computing, storage, and repository resources as needed for their project work.
Best practices for Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD), including automated testing be used as a key component of governance of these projects. Projects that follow these practices benefit from streamlined review for Authorization to Operate (ATO)
Data science and scientific teams can submit a single request for install and access to desktop tools and supporting environments, including cloud environments, git repositories, on premises server access, desktop software (ex: Python, VS Code, R Studio, Docker, git), etc.

Key architectural elements: 
Availability of Desktop, Cloud, and on-Premises Resources – Proposed architecture provides the three environments while accommodating various computing and security requirements. This includes on-premises high-performance computing infrastructure for more cost-effective operation of AI models or for handling use cases involving protected data.

Building off best practices described in the reference material section at the end of this document, a proposal for an advanced data science environment has been developed. Core to the spirit of this environment is flexibility: meaning that developers and data scientists should be enabled to provision resources for their own projects using provided templates and guides so that they can be responsive to requests while also respecting appropriate policies and governance.

Any integration with the Health Canada network should be carefully planned to ensure secure and seamless connectivity and data transfer. Best Practices in Advanced Data Science
A review of practices among other data science units within the Government of Canada Data Science Network was undertaken. These articles describe best practices from data science units in other government departments. Among the best practices described were the use of tools for developing and deploying production level software and effective use of MLOps principles (Chiumera, 2023; Gajjar et al., 2022; Kuehn, 2021; Montero, 2021; Singh, 2023; Treasury Board Secretariat, 2020). Among the principles discussed were the following:
Importance of Version Control: Version control tools, using platforms such as GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, and Azure DevOps enable teams to develop software together. These tools, if fully utilized, can facilitate tracking changes in the code, issue tracking, code reviews, and Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD), among other features.
Containerization: The use of containerization tools, such as Docker, enables developers to specify the runtime environment needed for their software. It allows the software to be flexible with respect to the hardware and operating system of the infrastructure that runs it. Containers can also be used in clusters, orchestrated using tools such as Kubernetes. The use of these tools enables flexibility and consistency in how the software is tested, deployed, and maintained.
Continuous Integration and Continuous Deployment (CI/CD): Practices and tools for automating the testing, building, and deployment of software. These tools are often integrated into version control tools such as GitHub, GitHub Enterprise, and Azure DevOps.
Emphasis on Testing: The development and maintenance of bulletproof code should include the development of test cases. These test cases help ensure that previous functionality is maintained as new functionality is added. This process should be supported by powerful testing frameworks, such as PyTest, and can be integrated into CI/CD pipelines.
Maintainability: An objective in designing software is to make it easy to maintain. Maintainability of software can often be expressed in terms of coupling and cohesion. Loosely coupled software means that a change in one part of the code does not break (or cause a need for changes) in other parts of the code. Highly cohesive code results from having different components (functions, classes, containers) responsible for the fewest number of concerns as possible. This separation of concerns provides for more reusable components.
Logging: The use of logging tools, which generate machine parseable logs, can be critical to detecting and resolving problems. Effective logging is also important for tracking experiments, models, and metrics. This can enable the detection of concept drift and model drift.

Proposal for HC OCDO Data Science use of SSC ICE
Bottom Line Up Front (BLUFF)
The HC OCDO is recommending the use of the on-premises computing offering by SSC ICE for performing prototyping as part of the options analysis for the RAG IT Project.
Summary
This document outlines the requirements for the RAG IT data science on-premises environment that delivers high-performance computing resources including GPUs, a secure and standardized software stack, containerization and orchestration capabilities, version control integration, flexible scaling options, and clear governance guardrails. This environment will empower data scientists with the autonomy, tools, and performance needed to innovate, experiment, and deliver impactful data-driven insights while maintaining security, policy compliance, and manageability.
An agile approach will be employed to test this environment by implementing a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) of the Retrieval Augmented Generative LLM experiment. A similar experiment was previously executed in the SSC Science Azure network.  This iterative process will focus on working closely with the SSC ICE team, learning and testing the HPC (High-Performance Computing) environment, allowing the CDO data science team to assess feasibility, identify gaps, and refine workflows rather than attempting to define all our on-prem requirements up front.
Computing Infrastructure Specifications
Modes of Operation
User Experience and Support 
The on-prem HPC environment will  support two distinct modes of operation to accommodate a different workflows and user preferences: batch submissions and interactive mode. These modes provide flexibility for users to either process large volumes of data efficiently or engage directly with the system for dynamic, real-time interactions. The following sections describe each mode in detail, outlining their features, benefits, and intended use cases as well as capacity management. 
Batch Submissions and Management
Users submit batch jobs via command-line tools, scripts, or APIs. These tasks run non-interactively, allowing long-running or parallel computations to execute efficiently without manual oversight.
The batch system dispatches tasks to a high-capacity server (or HPC cluster) that can distribute computations across multiple nodes or cores, returning results when execution is complete.
The batch system is configured and optimized for running large, parallelizable workloads more efficiently than interactive nodes.
Users can specify job parameters (e.g., number of CPUs/GPUs, memory requirements, queue priority) and rely on the scheduler to allocate resources optimally.
Compute tasks run autonomously, and users retrieve logs, outputs, and results upon completion.
Interactive Mode
User Interface and Access
Provide a command-line interface (CLI) for users to access and control the environment, set up, and run their experiments. If available, supplement the CLI with browser-based or remote desktop-like interfaces for accessing one or more interactive HPC nodes. Users can log in via secure methods (e.g., SSH, web-based portal) and immediately see available tools, graphical interfaces (e.g. Jupyter Notebooks, RStudio), and resource status. The CLI will allow users to perform tasks such as launching jobs, monitoring performance, and managing workflows directly from their terminal, complementing the graphical interface and catering to power users who prefer or require scriptable, text-based interaction. This dual-interface approach ensures flexibility and ease of use across diverse user preferences and requirements.
Offer interactive sessions where users can launch and run data science applications, notebooks, or development environments with the ability to visualize results, debug code, or tune models directly.
Capacity
When users request resources (CPU, memory, GPU) through a web or command-line interface they  are automatically placed in a queue if resources are not immediately available.
Provide real-time feedback on job status (e.g., pending, running, completed) and expected start times based on current resource utilization by other internal and external users.
Roles and Responsibilities
SSC responsible for: 
Provisioning and maintaining the HPC infrastructure, including hardware, operating systems, and core software libraries;
Manage user account users accounts and access controls, security and system monitoring; 
Resource panning and scheduling; 
Provide technical and user support; 
Provides polices and guidelines.
Provide governance and security oversight. 
Work closely with clients to gather feedback and identify opportunities to enhance services and provide users with as much control as possible ensuring they align with user needs.
Data Science Team responsible for:
Determination, implementation and monitoring of computing tasks; 
Select computational modes and resources and monitoring progress. 
Provide feedback on environment and performance. 
Provide feedback on the SSC team’s services, responsibilities, and performance to help refine offerings and improve collaboration.
RAGnalysis IT Minimal Viable Product Test
Phase I: Perform a quick test replicating a RAGnalysis IT MVP (Minimum Viable Product) experiment in the on-premises HPC cluster. The goal is to validate the feasibility, performance, and integration complexity of a retrieval-based LLM workflow running within a secure, high-throughput on-prem computing environment.


The Architectural Design diagram (above) captures the RAG IT experiment as it was executed in an Azure cloud environment and therefore includes Azure-specific components such as Azure AI Hub, and Azure Container Registry. This diagram serves as a representative architecture, illustrating the logical flow and interactions between components during the experiment. In the transition of the experiment to an ICE-based solution, the Azure components will be replaced with ICE-available equivalents, ensuring that the overall structure and functionality remain consistent while aligning with the ICE  capabilities and standards.

General Purpose Science Cluster for HICC

The OCDO-Data Science Team (DST) is requesting the purchase of SSC’s General Purpose Science Cluster (GPSC) for 2024 onward. 
Background
SSC provides High Performance Computing capacity via their GPSC to government departments. HICC is requesting access to one 128 core node with 128 GB of RAM and 5TB of storage. This will allow HICC data science users across the department and the AI Centre of Expertise to run jobs that require compute capacity above what is available on laptops or tablets. 
The targeted use of GPSC is for data processing and data science and geospatial activities that take over 16GB of RAM and/or requires processing of over 10 GB of data. Our current capacity cannot support heavy data science work on imagery data or large text files. This prevents us from being able to operationalize planned use cases such as ChatBots and Large Language Models (LLM) to support faster access to curated program information (Horizontal Results and Reporting project) and Digital Twins for more informed decision making and program evaluation (Major Bridges Pilot). 
This offering by SSC was deemed the most suitable option to increase compute capacity in the department by the Cloud Services Team. Data Science Team has been piloting an LLM and Chatbot with Horizontal Results and Reporting, using the GPSC. Testing over the summer has indicated the GPSC meets all our current and foreseeable AI capacity needs.
Cost
The initial set up cost is $137,608, which includes the one time set up fee and the annual maintenance fee of $3,118. 

Platform features and operations


The SSC clusters offer multiple nodes with high-core-count Xeon processors. The nodes are suited for handling large datasets, running complex tasks (including graphical processing tasks such as imagery data), and training deep learning models that require significant computational resources. For example, one of the computers available for use features a 3072 GB of RAM.  
 
In particular, SSC offers two powerful capabilities. The first is an interactive system for normal workloads. This system offers multiple interactive nodes (computers) that allow users to run graphical tools and applications interactively. Capacity is only used for the job scheduled. Jobs are queued and run based on nodes available given how the resources are used by other projects both internal to HICC and external users on the platform. Even in this interactive capacity, the HPC option is still superior to our current capacity in terms of memory, CPU, etc. 
 
The SSC cluster also offers a non-interactive, general-purpose system (know as Batch system): this system allows users to run parallel tasks efficiently. In this system, tasks are scheduled and sent to an external high-capacity server that responds back with execution. 

HICC data scientist will interact with GPSC in the following, illustrated manner:

Roles and Responsibilities
The overall roles and responsibilities are such that SSC in charge of all aspects of the HPC platform, whereas HICC is responsible for the data, code, pipelines and containers on the platform.


Considerations
Capacity
There is a set amount of space (though large) where we could run out of space in the long run. However, SSC is continually upgrading their capacity and service offerings to meet demand. 
Queuing system 
The batch system mentioned above uses a queuing approach: jobs are executed based on priority which is defined through parameters that admins control. This means that capacity may not be available on demand. This could be problematic for production workloads. 
 
Drag, drop, download, upload
Given that we currently use SharePoint as document repository, and since the SSC nodes are outside to our system, most of the tasks we perform would require manual file exchange between the two systems. This limits automation of certain routine tasks such as scheduled runs (e.g. is the scheduled tasks we used to run for the PAU project). 

Onboarding
The SSC cluster is built on Linux & uses the Ubuntu operating system. This may require some learning. The DST is committed to training their own team, however, will have limited capacity to onboard other HICC users.  
Recommended Infrastructure
The GPSC was determined as the best option via a Business Requirement from HICC Cloud Services Team to SSC based on our requirements.  

Recommended uses

Given the HICC AI ambition over the next few years targets the growth in AI within the domains of in innovation, testing, and internal operations, the recommended uses of this HPC are internal:
Innovation
Experimentation
Research and policy development
Not time sensitive production (repetitive use) 
As of fall 2024, any work must use only up to Protected A data and follow HICC security protocols and privacy standards. 
Protect B projects can be considered once SSC has established procedures for Protect B workloads. 
HICC AI activities to grow and develop support of tools and systems for external facing services and operations are not expected until 2026-27. This will provide us with time to assess the needs and the ever-changing technological requirements for this type of activities. 

Current Use Cases
Results Reporting LLM
Project Objectives
 
The pilot project will use a large language model (“LLM”) to conduct analysis of HICC unprotected program data, specifically projects titles and project descriptions, to produce project-level results outputs aligned with INFC’s business lines and core indicators. 
These outputs will help narrow the existing result gap on legacy and existing programs by providing a more comprehensive understanding of (1) HICC and (2) CCBF investments. The data obtained will also enable future trend analysis with external data, including the CCPI. 
 
Business Outcome

The immediate outcomes of the project are (1) the collection of Core Indicators results data, from HICC and CCBF not classified or protected project descriptions; and (2) pilot test Generative Artificial Intelligence capacity for the department by demonstrating technology feasibility and cost efficiency. 
 
In the intermediate term, trend analysis on the extracted results data could be conducted, including comparison with CCPI survey data.  
 
Project Scope
 
The pilot project will analyze CIP-provided datasets comprised of project data from (1) the Infrastructure Funding Reports since 2002 (19,000 projects) and (2) CCBF’s Master Project List since 2014/15 (71,000 projects). These datasets will be queried against a fixed list of core indicators and select indicators to identify some of the expected project results.

The custom dataset would only comprise of data that is not classified or protected in some capacity. This includes, but not limited to: (1) the Government of Canada’s open data portal, (2) HICC’s Housing and Infrastructure Project Map, (3) funding announcements, and (4) CCBF delivery partner reporting.  
 
Generative AI may also be used to search the Internet to verify the accuracy of HICC and CCBF project descriptions, and identify discrepancies for quality assurance.

Phase 1 will take place in fall 2024 and phase 2 will take place winter 2025, pending any ATO changes that may be necessary for CCBF’s unclassified (but not open) data. 

Digital Twin proposal for Samuel De Champlain Bridge Corridor
Background
A digital twin is a virtual representation of a physical object or system designed to reflect the real-world counterpart accurately. Digital Twins support data-driven decision making, scenario testing, and evaluation of assets that are impacted or contribute to increasingly complex systems, networks and socio-economic outcomes. 
Business Value
We are proposing to build a Digital Twin for the Samuel De Champlain Bridge Corridor to:
Monitor bridge health by predicting potential failures and opportunities for improvement
Inform decision making on bridge maintenance through scenario building and testing,
Connect the Samuel De Champlain Bridge Corridor to housing, resilient infrastructure and other HICC program outcomes.  
Feasibility
The Samuel De Champlain Bridge Corridor is not only poised to reap the benefits of a Digital Twin for monitoring bridge health, analyzing impacts to lane closures or disruptions, preparing for the Gordy Howe operations, but it also is well positioned to provide the quality, curated data necessary to create a Digital Twin. 
The following table outlines the high level components, and their availability at HICC, to create a Digital Twin. 

PRB – Geospatial Processing Climate and Infrastructure

Project Objectives

The primary objective of this project is to leverage High-Performance Computing (HPC) to enhance geospatial data processing, specifically for flood risk analysis and infrastructure assessment. By using HPC resources, the goal is to significantly reduce the time it takes to visualize and process large datasets. A proposed pilot project will utilize QGIS to map high-resolution flood areas at the dissemination area geographic level across the country. This will help assess the regions at highest risk of flooding, as well as the infrastructure value and population demographics within those areas. 
The success of this pilot will be measured by the ability to join flood data tables, which can be as large as 4GB, with dissemination area census data. If the join can be completed successfully within 8 hours, the pilot will be considered a success. A positive outcome will enable the joined geometry dataset to include both flood data and dissemination area census information. Subsequent steps will involve using the HPC environment to analyze other climate hazard data. The project also aims to apply this capability across various analyses by working-level analysts from the Data & Analytics Division, particularly in flood data and transportation planning.

Business Outcome
This project aims to provide significant improvements in processing efficiency, enabling quicker insights into flood risk assessments and infrastructure evaluation. By reducing the time required for spatial data analysis, HICC can respond more rapidly to potential climate-related hazards and improve its overall decision-making processes.

Project Scope

The scope of this project includes the use of QGIS within the HPC environment to process and analyze geospatial flood data at high resolution, with the goal of joining flood data tables and dissemination area census data to assess flood risk and associated infrastructure. Several working-level analysts from the Data & Analytics Division will be engaged in using the HPC environment to perform these analyses, with a focus on flood data but also with potential applications in transportation planning. If successful, the project will proceed with further use of the HPC environment to analyze other climate hazard data.

Report on Health Canada’s Data Science Infrastructure Needs



Executive Summary
Shared Services Canada’s (SSC) Infrastructure Research and Innovation (IRI) has engaged Shared Services Canada’s Artificial Intelligence Program (AIP) to assist with defining Health Canada’s (HC) requirements for a data science environment.  HC’s data scientists face challenges in accessing scalable, flexible computing resources to support interactive development, long-running processes, and software development. 
Three core themes emerged from discussions:
The need for an interactive data science environment – A flexible workspace to conduct experiments, visualize results, and iterate on models and code.
The need for an environment to execute long-running software processes – Reliable, scalable resources for computationally intensive batch workloads.
The need for a software development environment – A controlled yet adaptable space for developing and maintaining AI/ML pipelines and applications.
To address these issues, a combination of platforms was proposed:
INSEE’s Onyxia Labs, which provides a containerized, interactive data science platform.
Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management (SLURM), a widely used workload manager for high-performance computing (HPC) that enables efficient scheduling and monitoring of batch jobs.
This report details the engagement process, the identified challenges, and potential solutions for enabling HC’s data science teams to work more effectively.
Engagement Overview
SSC and HC met in a series of meetings through December to March (2024/2025).  HC staff responded to a structured questionnaire of needs and also produced documentation to describe their team’s initiatives.  SSC’s Science Program hosted a multiple stakeholder meeting on March 7th that prominently featured HC’s requirements.
A range of issues were explored in meetings including:
How does HC currently carry out their work?  What are the limitations of current methods?
How does SSC support data science efforts within the Government of Canada.
What technology exists to assist data scientists at Health Canada.
Participants
During the discussions, comments were gathered from HC, SSC, Statistics Canada, and the Department of Fisheries and Oceans (DFO). Key stakeholders from HC included Patrick Gavigan, Charles Kemp, Christopher Pollard, and Annette Dodge.
Key participants at SSC included Brian McKittrick, Justin Maheux, Olesia Kazantseva, Scott Syms, Peter Boyd, and Ian Stitt.
Problem Statement: Challenges Faced by Data Scientists
HC’s data science team face significant roadblocks in executing their work efficiently. The main challenges identified include:
Infrastructure Limitations:
Inability to quickly spin up computing environments for analysis.
Lack of persistent workspaces for data science projects.
Limited access to high-performance computing resources.
Process and Compliance Barriers:
Lengthy approval and provisioning times for cloud-based tools.
Stringent security and governance requirements (e.g., Protected B classification).
Complex Authorization to Operate (ATO) processes, leading to increased costs and delays.
Tooling and Resource Constraints:
Need for flexible software environments (e.g., Jupyter, RStudio, VS Code).
Lack of clear governance on AI/ML model deployment.
Expiring cloud-based workspaces leading to data loss and workflow disruptions.
Key Themes Identified
Interactive Data Science Environment
HC’s data scientists require an on-demand, self-service environment for experimentation and development. This environment should:
Provide access to Jupyter Notebooks, RStudio, and Python-based toolkits.
Allow seamless integration with GitHub/GitLab for version control.
Enable persistent workspaces that do not expire arbitrarily.
Be deployable in on-premises and cloud environments for flexibility.
Provide tool and library provenance to ensure security guardrails.
Allow for persistent projects.
Provide version management and archiving of interactive work.
Allow for GPU and CPU, multi-node workflows.
The ability to process HC data up to Protected B.
Execution Environment for Long-Running Processes
Data science workflows frequently involve batch processing of large datasets, requiring:
A robust workload management system to schedule and prioritize jobs.
The ability to queue, manage, and monitor long-running tasks.
Resources that support GPU-accelerated workloads.
The ability to report on process status and log execution.
Software Development Environment
A controlled yet flexible software development environment is needed for DS/AI/ML engineering:
Containerization tools (Docker, Kubernetes) for packaging AI applications.
Integrated CI/CD pipelines for model deployment.
Granular permissions to allow controlled installation of additional libraries.
Code management tools to support versioning in iterative development.
Provide tool and library curation to ensure security guardrails.
Universality of Themes in the GC
HC’s concerns resonate across the GC. Many GC data scientists are in search of machine learning development environments that allow processing of Protected B data. However, only a fortunate few departments have access to cloud-based data science tools, and even among these, only a handful possess the necessary accreditations required to handle protected data within these environments. Typically, it's the larger departments that have achieved this level of capability.
GC software developers share these complaints due to the overlap in tools used by developers and data scientists.
Given the need the solution we develop for Health Canada data science may be of interest by other departmental AI teams.
Our recommendations focus on widely-used data science tools that are standard in the industry, including VSCode, Python, GIT, and Jupyter Notebooks.   

Proposed Solutions
Interactive Development Environment and Prototyping Platform
INSEE’s Onyxia Labs is a containerized data science environment built on Kubernetes, designed to provide an interactive workspace for data scientists. 
GitLab is a DevOps platform that provides source code management, CI/CD, security, and collaboration tools in a single application. It supports Git repositories, issue tracking, code review, and automation, enabling teams to develop, secure, and deploy software efficiently.  It is an analogue of Microsoft’s GitHub.
Both products can be installed on a single instance of Kubernetes to provide self-serve configurable environments for data science and software prototyping.  This combination can be placed on a single machine to serve as a development appliance or installed on a centrally in a public or private cloud environment.
Features & Capabilities:
Pre-configured environments for Python, R, and other AI/ML tools.
Containerized applications ensuring reproducibility and consistency.
Flexible deployment – available both on-premises and in the cloud.
Integrated access control allowing organizations to manage user permissions.
Potential Benefits for Health Canada:
Enables a self-service model for data scientists to quickly spin up pin up their environments.
Provides persistence across sessions, preventing work loss.
Supports collaborative development, including Git integration.
Allows compliance with Protected B requirements through on-premises hosting.
Provides an isolated development environment for software development.

Long running batch processes
SLURM (Simple Linux Utility for Resource Management) is an open-source workload manager commonly used in High Performance Computing environments (including SSC’s HPC platform) to manage large-scale computing tasks.
It queues and executes long-running jobs within a framework when resources are free.
Key Features:
Job Scheduling & Queuing: Efficiently schedules batch jobs and allocates compute resources.
Scalability: Supports clusters ranging from small labs to large supercomputers.
GPU & CPU Resource Management: Allows fine-grained control over computation.
Integration with AI/ML Pipelines: Enables automation of machine learning workloads.
How SLURM Addresses HC’s Needs:
Enables efficient execution of long-running batch processes.
Reduces the need for manual resource allocation, improving efficiency.
Supports high-performance computing (HPC) use cases, including deep learning.
Provides fair-share scheduling to allocate resources equitably among users.

Next Steps
Pending approval of these recommendations, we propose installing Onyxia Labs in ICELab and create a series of UNCLAS data science and software development tasks to evaluate the platform.
After this work, we could proceed with a similar evaluation of SLURM in ICELab.

Proposal for HC OCDO Data Science use of SSC ICE
Bottom Line Up Front (BLUFF)
The HC OCDO is recommending the use of the on-premises computing offering by SSC ICELab for performing prototyping as part of the options analysis for the RAG IT Project.
Summary
This document outlines the requirements for the RAG IT data science on-premises environment that delivers high-performance computing resources including GPUs, a secure and standardized software stack, containerization and orchestration capabilities, version control integration, flexible scaling options, and clear governance guardrails. This environment will empower data scientists with the autonomy, tools, and performance needed to innovate, experiment, and deliver impactful data-driven insights while maintaining security, policy compliance, and manageability.
An agile approach will be employed to test this environment by implementing a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) of the Retrieval Augmented Generative LLM experiment. A similar experiment was previously executed in the SSC Science Azure network.  This iterative process will focus on working closely with the SSC ICE team, learning and testing the HPC (High-Performance Computing) environment, allowing the CDO data science team to assess feasibility, identify gaps, and refine workflows rather than attempting to define all our on-prem requirements up front.
Computing Infrastructure Specifications
Modes of Operation
User Experience and Support 
The on-prem HPC environment will  support two distinct modes of operation to accommodate a different workflows and user preferences: batch submissions and interactive mode. These modes provide flexibility for users to either process large volumes of data efficiently or engage directly with the system for dynamic, real-time interactions. The following sections describe each mode in detail, outlining their features, benefits, and intended use cases as well as capacity management. 
Batch Submissions and Management
Users submit batch jobs via command-line tools, scripts, or APIs. These tasks run non-interactively, allowing long-running or parallel computations to execute efficiently without manual oversight.
The batch system dispatches tasks to a high-capacity server (or HPC cluster) that can distribute computations across multiple nodes or cores, returning results when execution is complete.
The batch system is configured and optimized for running large, parallelizable workloads more efficiently than interactive nodes.
Users can specify job parameters (e.g., number of CPUs/GPUs, memory requirements, queue priority) and rely on the scheduler to allocate resources optimally.
Compute tasks run autonomously, and users retrieve logs, outputs, and results upon completion.
Interactive Mode
User Interface and Access
Provide a command-line interface (CLI) for users to access and control the environment, set up, and run their experiments. If available, supplement the CLI with browser-based or remote desktop-like interfaces for accessing one or more interactive HPC nodes. Users can log in via secure methods (e.g., SSH, web-based portal) and immediately see available tools, graphical interfaces (e.g. Jupyter Notebooks, RStudio), and resource status. The CLI will allow users to perform tasks such as launching jobs, monitoring performance, and managing workflows directly from their terminal, complementing the graphical interface and catering to power users who prefer or require scriptable, text-based interaction. This dual-interface approach ensures flexibility and ease of use across diverse user preferences and requirements.
Offer interactive sessions where users can launch and run data science applications, notebooks, or development environments with the ability to visualize results, debug code, or tune models directly.
Capacity
When users request resources (CPU, memory, GPU) through a web or command-line interface they  are automatically placed in a queue if resources are not immediately available.
Provide real-time feedback on job status (e.g., pending, running, completed) and expected start times based on current resource utilization by other internal and external users.
